title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 6: Holmes, Money and Trust
keywords: New Code of Judicial Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary
Code of Conduct for Judicial Personnel
Ramon Magsaysay Award for Government Service
Philippine Judicial Academy complex in Tagaytay
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- a keynote address to a business audience built on a chance-met banker's Holmes quotation, 'Do not put your trust in your money. Rather, put your money in trust,' which CJP turns into an argument that the Supreme Court's only currency is public trust.

A defense of the Court against the charge that it interferes inordinately with national economic policy, grounded in his own Mining Law decision and in Tanada v. Angara, and in the distinction between reviewing economic wisdom (which the Court refuses) and correcting grave abuse of discretion (which it is duty-bound to do).

The evidence of trust: Makati Business Club and Social Weather Stations surveys ranking the Court among the country's five most trusted institutions, and Congress's obedience to the ruling voiding the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide.

A working tour of the Action Program for Judicial Reform, organized as a transformation of the judges themselves -- selection, education, ethics, compensation, discipline and reward -- and then of the environment in which they work: courthouses, computerization, docket unclogging, new rules and information campaigns.
sub_topics: CJP opens with a concert at the Carlos P. Romulo Auditorium where he sat beside Richard Holmes of American Express International, who quoted the Justice Holmes line displayed in his office about money and trust.
He contrasts business, whose main concern is honestly earned money, with the Supreme Court, whose necessary capital is the continuing trust of the populace.

Decisions, he insists, are not crafted for popularity: cases are won or lost on reasoned arguments flowing from legal principles and precedents, not on palatability, compromise, friendship or pecuniary consideration.
Yet the Court is not averse to public opinion, because it has no army or police to enforce its decisions, no money to exact loyalty, and no inclination to mount rallies.

He draws the key distinction between the shifting winds of public emotion and long-term institutional trust -- critics may disagree with specific rulings but should concede the Court's good faith, wisdom, probity and diligence.
He confronts the criticism that the Court has no business expertise and should not reverse economic actions of the political branches.

He quotes at length the 246-page Mining Law decision he wrote: the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes, the President and Congress must be given maximum discretion, and the Court must not interfere inordinately and unnecessarily.

He traces that restraint back to Tanada v. Angara (1997), also his ponencia, where the Court refused to annul the Senate's concurrence in the WTO Treaty and said the wisdom of the choice was outside judicial review.

He answers the critics who cite the AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA-PACIFIC annulments: those contracts violated the Constitution, public-bidding laws and the agencies' own regulations, and reeked of corruption -- one being labeled 'the grandmother of all scams.'

The resulting rule: the Court does not render economic decisions but judgments on how law applies to any field of human endeavor, and it must 'interfere' only when officials blatantly violate the law or act with grave abuse of discretion.
Independent Makati Business Club and Social Weather Stations surveys consistently place the Supreme Court among the top five most trusted institutions in the country.

The severest test of that trust was the ruling that the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide was unconstitutional; Congress, albeit reluctantly, obeyed, and President Arroyo hailed this as proof of the system's viability.
CJP clarifies that the outcome did not make the Court superior to Congress or the President -- only that the Constitution was supreme and binding on all officials as the Court interprets it.
He turns to reform: the 'Davide Watch' of November 30, 1998 and the APJR approved December 8, 2000, with six components covering judges and judicial institutions alike.

The APJR has drawn grants from the World Bank, ADB, UNDP and The Asia Foundation plus aid from Australia, Britain, Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, the United States and the European Union, and the World Bank posts it on its own website as a model.
Transformation of judges begins upstream: law-curriculum upgrading and law schools placed under a Board of Legal Education under the Supreme Court's aegis, plus reform of the bar examinations.

Selection and formation: required years of practice, transparent and rigid Judicial and Bar Council screening with three nominees per vacancy, a pre-judicature program, continuing judicial education, and the P600 million Philja complex in Tagaytay negotiated with JICA.

Ethics: the New Code of Judicial Conduct and the Code of Conduct for Judicial Personnel, effective June 1, 2004, taking off from the Bangalore Draft agreed at the Hague Judicial Round-Table of November 25-26, 2002.
Compensation: Congress doubled judicial pay through a 25 percent annual increase over four years beginning November 6, 2003.

Discipline and reward: 262 justices, judges and court personnel and 119 lawyers were penalized in one year, while the Judicial Excellence Awards honor awardees year-round, and Davide funded employee awards from his 2002 Ramon Magsaysay Award prize.

Upgrading the environment, first: courthouse construction and renovation and the Pilot E-Court Program in Branch 140 of the Makati RTC, with three more model electronic courts in Angeles, Lapu Lapu and Cagayan de Oro.

Second, computerization: the SC website, the USAID-backed Case Flow Management pilot in Pasay City, the CIDA-funded CAMIS, the Electronic Judicial Library launched November 19, 2004 holding all decisions from 1901, and a computer-literacy program for 28,000 officials and employees.
Third, unclogging dockets by promoting mediation, arbitration and conciliation, given that one third of trial courts are vacant because of low pay.

Fourth and fifth, new rules on intellectual property, electronic evidence, corporate rehabilitation, pretrial, discovery, family problems and violence against women and children; and information campaigns including Chamber-to-Chamber Dialogues and EU-supported Access to Justice for the Poor.

International recognition: visiting jurists from Bhutan, Nepal, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the APJR's citation as a model by World Bank and UN speakers at the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch, October 4-8, 2001.

He closes by returning to Holmes, assuring the business audience that they can put their trust in the Supreme Court, which will protect their investments by leveling the business playing field and promoting the rule of law.

stances.claim: The Supreme Court's effectiveness rests entirely on public trust, because it has no army or police to enforce its decisions, no money to exact loyalty, and no inclination to mount rallies to incite obedience.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from institutional powerlessness: the Court's lack of coercive means is offered as proof that trust is not optional but structural

stances.claim: The Court does not render economic decisions and does not sit in judgment on the wisdom of the political branches' economic policy; it renders judgments on how laws are applied, and intervenes only when officials blatantly violate the Constitution or the law or act with grave abuse of discretion.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-quotation as proof: two of his own ponencias, the Mining Law decision and Tanada v. Angara, are quoted at length to show the doctrine in operation rather than merely asserted

stances.claim: The AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA-PACIFIC annulments were not inordinate interference: those contracts violated specific constitutional provisions, public-bidding laws and the executing agencies' own regulations, and reeked of corruption.
stances.rhetorical_move: rebuttal by supplying the omitted facts -- 'what our critics have conveniently neglected to say' -- followed by the corruption findings the Court itself made

stances.claim: When the Court voided the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide and Congress obeyed, the result did not make the Court superior to Congress or the President; it signified only that the Constitution was supreme and binding on all officials.
stances.rhetorical_move: disclaiming the victory: a ruling in the Court's own favor is reframed as the supremacy of the Constitution rather than of the institution

stances.claim: The APJR is a credible reform blueprint rather than an aspiration, as shown by unqualified support from the world's major development agencies and by the World Bank's posting of it as a model for other developing nations.
stances.rhetorical_move: external validation: third-party endorsement and donor money are marshalled as evidence of a domestic program's seriousness

notable_anecdotes: Three weeks before the speech, CJP and his wife attended a concert at the Carlos P. Romulo Auditorium of the RCBC Center in Makati, where he was seated beside visiting banker Richard Holmes of American Express International and struck up a conversation by mentioning Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
The banker replied that a Holmes quotation hung in his office -- 'Do not put your trust in your money. Rather, put your money in trust' -- which became the organizing conceit of the entire address.

He recalls writing the 246-page decision upholding the constitutionality of the Mining Law, quoting its instruction that the Constitution be read in broad, life-giving strokes and not used to strangulate economic growth.

He recounts that in one annulled mega-contract the Court ordered the ombudsman and the solicitor general to determine the criminal and civil liabilities of the officials concerned, and that another transaction was labeled 'the grandmother of all scams.'

He reports that Chief Justice Davide set aside the earnings from his 2002 Ramon Magsaysay Award cash prize to fund awards for court personnel below the rank of clerk of court, with the first ceremonies due December 15.

He notes that as chair of the Judicial Excellence Awards committee he announced on September 17 that awardees would be honored year-round, given roles in lectures and public fora, made role models and recommended for promotion.

He mentions jurists from Bhutan, Nepal, Vietnam and Indonesia coming to observe Philippine judicial reforms, and the APJR being cited as a model by World Bank and UN speakers in Christchurch in October 2001.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a keynote address to the Philippine Business Forum / Economist Corporate Network that Justice Panganiban built around a chance encounter three weeks earlier at a concert in Makati, where he sat beside Richard Holmes of American Express International, who quoted a line displayed in his office and attributed to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.: do not put your trust in your money, but rather put your money in trust. Business, CJP said, is about honestly earned money; the Supreme Court needs trust, because it has no army or police to enforce its decisions, no money to exact loyalty, and no inclination to mount rallies. Decisions are won or lost on reasoned arguments flowing from legal principles and precedents, not on popular palatability, yet the Court must retain the long-term trust of the public as distinct from the shifting winds of public emotion. He then answered the charge that the Court interferes inordinately with economic policy, quoting at length his own 246-page Mining Law decision -- the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes, not used to strangulate economic growth, and the Court must restrain itself from intruding into policy matters -- and his 1997 ponencia in Tanada v. Angara, which refused to annul the Senate's concurrence in the WTO Treaty because the wisdom of that choice lay outside judicial review. The AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA-PACIFIC annulments, he argued, involved contracts that violated the Constitution, bidding laws and the agencies' own regulations and reeked of corruption, one being called the grandmother of all scams. He cited Makati Business Club and Social Weather Stations surveys ranking the Court among the five most trusted institutions, and Congress's reluctant obedience to the ruling voiding the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide, clarifying that this showed the supremacy of the Constitution and not of the Court. He then surveyed the Action Program for Judicial Reform -- judge selection, education, ethics, doubled compensation, discipline and awards, courthouse construction, e-courts, computerization, the e-library, alternative dispute resolution, new rules and information campaigns -- and closed by assuring his audience that they could put their trust in the Supreme Court.
